newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn plans no big cuts in aid to east - deputy.
newsitem.headline: Bonn plans no big cuts in aid to east - deputy.

text.p: Germany has no plans to cut aid to its formerly communist eastern states by 4.5 billion marks next year, a key parliamentarian said on Thursday, denying media reports.
"Someone was talking nonsense yesterday," said Paul Krueger, spokesman for Christian Democrat parliamentarians from eastern states.
"I believe we do not need to fear cuts anywhere near the size being discussed," Krueger said in a radio interview.
"No one is telling us we have to find drastic further savings. Even if that were the case, I cannot imagine that the east would be disproportionately affected," he said.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, straining to rein in Germany's budget deficit to qualify for the single European currency, has been scraping every corner of the federal budget for possible spending cuts.
Waigel is due to present his budget for 1998 to the cabinet on July 11, and is expected to propose a supplementary budget for 1997 at the same time.
Bernhard Vogel, premier of the eastern state of Thuringia, threatened "most massive resistance" against the planned spending cuts if the reports prove to be true.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition has made commitments to maintain transfers to the eastern states at about the current level until 2004 in an effort to boost jobs in the region, where unemployment is far higher than in the west.
Such transfers have averaged 130 billion to 140 billion marks a year since unification in 1990, not counting the 450 billion marks in old eastern debt that Bonn absorbed, Waigel said this week.
Krueger and Vogel said pressure to cut spending in the east was coming from Germany's southern states, particularly Bavaria, but that the majority of Germans see the need to maintain it.
